fieldFixes.contribution: On 31 October 2008 a person or group writing as Satoshi Nakamoto announced 'a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party' on the Cryptography mailing list and published the Bitcoin white paper, which uses a proof-of-work system 'similar to Adam Back's Hashcash' and cites Wei Dai's b-money. Because every transaction is announced publicly, the paper abandoned the banking model of privacy through restricted access and proposed instead to keep public keys unlinked to identities, recommending a new key pair for each transaction while conceding that some linking was unavoidable. The author's identity has never been established; in 2024 the High Court of England and Wales declared that Craig Wright, who had claimed the role, is not Satoshi Nakamoto.

This later consequentials judgment records both. fieldFixes.contribution: Marlinspike's mobile-security company Whisper Systems was acquired by Twitter in late 2011; Twitter released some of its software under the GPLv3 licence, and in January 2013 he launched a new home for the community project continuing that work, which he called Open Whisper Systems. issues: All quotes re-fetched fresh and found verbatim. The thread quote ('any given disclosure will be, within a small multiplicative factor, just as likely whether or not the individual participates in the database') is FOUND in the ICALP PDF. Harvard SEAS is dated January 8, 2025 and says she received the medal 'last week'. NPR's datePublished is 2026-06-12.

The contribution credits the 2006 results to Dwork alone ('Dwork showed ... and proposed instead differential privacy'). Her own acknowledgements say: 'The impossibility result is joint work with Moni Naor ... The definition, the differential privacy mechanism, and Theorems 4 and 5 are joint work with Frank McSherry.' The co-credit is added and the acknowledgement is added as a source.

The influence line says the 2026 Commerce order banned noise infusion 'including differential privacy'. NPR and the Census Bureau page describe the order as banning 'noise infusion' and do not name differential privacy. The Census page does say the 2020 noise was applied 'using a newer protection framework based on “differential privacy”' and that its DP page 'is no longer current' because of the order. The wording is tightened so it does not attribute the words 'differential privacy' to the order.

fieldFixes.contribution: Working at Microsoft Research, Dwork showed in 2006 — in an impossibility result she credits as joint work with Moni Naor — that the long-standing goal for statistical databases, that nothing about an individual be learnable that could not be learned without the database, cannot be achieved, and proposed instead 'differential privacy', a definition she credits as joint work with Frank McSherry: any given disclosure should be almost equally likely whether or not a person's data are included. With colleagues she developed methods that add calibrated random noise to statistics to meet that guarantee. The technique is used by Apple on its devices and was the basis of the Disclosure Avoidance System for the 2020 US Census; she received the US National Medal of Science in January 2025.
fieldFixes.influence: Differential privacy moved privacy protection from promises about data handling to a measurable mathematical guarantee; it was the backbone of the 2020 US Census's disclosure avoidance, although in 2026 the US Commerce Department ordered the Census Bureau to stop using 'noise infusion', the method on which its differential-privacy protections rely.

fieldFixes.contribution: Sweeney showed that 'anonymised' records could be re-identified by linking them to public data: for twenty dollars she bought the Cambridge, Massachusetts voter list and matched it to supposedly de-identified state-employee medical data, finding Governor William Weld's records because, of the six voters who shared his birth date, only three were men and he was the only one in his five-digit ZIP code. issues: All quotes re-fetched fresh and found verbatim: the cr.yp.to problem and status pages, 176 F.3d 1132 ('Decided May 6, 1999'), the 192 F.3d 1308 order ('Filed September 30, 1999') and the EFF case page.

Wrong date: 'the case ended in 2002'. The 18 October 2002 date on the status page is the oral argument at which the government backed away from its regulations. Bernstein's own press release of 15 October 2003 (https://cr.yp.to/export/2003/10.15-bernstein.txt, the last item in his chronological documents list) reports that Chief Judge Marilyn Hall Patel 'dismissed Bernstein's case without deciding the constitutionality of the current regulations'. The case ended in October 2003.

Checked and correct: doctoral candidate at UC Berkeley; he asked the State Department whether he needed a licence and was told Snuffle was a munition under ITAR; district court rulings in December 1996 (ITAR) and August 1997 (EAR); panel opinion on 6 May 1999; withdrawn for en banc rehearing on 30 Sep 1999; new exception in January 2000; lawsuit filed February 1995 (per the 2003 press release).

fieldFixes.contribution: As a doctoral candidate at UC Berkeley, Bernstein devised an encryption method he called Snuffle and asked whether he needed a licence to publish its description and source code; the State Department said it was a 'munition' under the arms-export rules. With lawyers backed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation he sued in February 1995, and the district court held in December 1996 and again in August 1997 that the regulations were unconstitutional. A Ninth Circuit panel agreed on 6 May 1999 that the export rules were a prior restraint on scientific expression, but that opinion was withdrawn for rehearing en banc; the government then loosened the rules in January 2000, and after it promised in October 2002 not to enforce several provisions, the district court dismissed the case in October 2003 as unripe, without a final ruling on the constitutionality of the current rules.
